extracted.intended_audience: Canadian patent examiners and patent applicants/agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on assessing novelty, obviousness, priority/claim date, grace period, double-patenting, selections, and related procedural matters in Canadian patent examination. Covers how examiners should analyze and what applicants should provide (priority documents, translations, arguments) for prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unexpected utility can support inventiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: In many cases, the ingenuity of an invention is related to its utility. This is particularly the case where some unexpected result is achieved through the subject-matter of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a known product/process modified to be useful for a new purpose or to provide an additional advantage; simplification that retains original utility. Unexpected result may support patentability where it shows inventive contribution rather than mere routine modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: New use of a known thing requires novelty and unobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the invention lies in discovering that a known thing has properties that make it useful for some new purpose, that mere discovery does not confer patentability on the known thing. The new use may be patented, however, if it is novel and unobvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "A patent for the mere new use of a known contrivance, without any additional ingenuity in overcoming fresh difficulties is bad and cannot be supported. If the new use involves no ingenuity, but is in manner and purpose analogous to the old use, although not quite the same, there is no invention." Applicants should show additional ingenuity or unexpectedness for new-use claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor variations and expected substitutions are obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor variations in existing inventions, such as the changing of size, shape, proportion or quality, where the result is merely the doing of 'the same thing in the same way, by substantially the same means, with better results, is not such an invention as will sustain a patent.' The substitution of a superior material for an inferior material, where the advantages of the substitution were expected, has similarly been found to be obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the advantage from a change or substitution was predictable from common general knowledge or the prior art, it will generally be considered obvious. Applicants must demonstrate something beyond predictable improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of known elements require a new unitary result
rubrics_metrics.description: "All the elements being old, and the functions to be performed being identical, [it can] be patentable only if it performed the old function in some better or cheaper way than did the earlier machines – there must be a new mode of operation resulting from the combination [...]; it is not invention to combine old devices in a new machine or manufacture without producing some new mode of operation..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent a new unitary result arising from their combination, an assemblage of known parts is merely an uninventive aggregation. Examiner should look for a new mode of operation or unitary technical effect when assessing combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish sound prediction (utility) from obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessment of utility and obviousness may be somewhat interdependent where the utility must be based on a sound prediction, particularly where information necessary to permit a person skilled in the art to soundly predict that a known thing would be useful forms part of the state of the art. Although in certain situations it may be that an invention either lacks sound prediction or is obvious, the assessment of sound prediction and the assessment of obviousness are distinct tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sound prediction is based on the applicant’s description and drawings, accepted scientific laws or principles and common general knowledge; obviousness is based on the state of the art. Examiners should apply distinct analyses and applicants should address both where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation often implies obviousness; use Sanofi four-step analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the subject-matter of a claim is considered to be anticipated by a prior art disclosure, it will often also be considered to be obvious. The existence of an anticipatory disclosure will typically lead to the conclusion at step 3 of the Sanofi obviousness analysis that there is no difference between the inventive concept of the claim and the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners need not provide separate analyses for anticipation and obviousness where a single analysis covers both, but may identify both defects later. Applicants responding to lack-of-novelty reports should explain why the subject-matter is unobvious and may use the Sanofi four-step approach when formulating arguments. If an impasse develops and Final Action is approaching, separate analyses for anticipation and obviousness should be provided at least one report before Final Action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim date = filing date unless compliant priority claim valid
rubrics_metrics.description: In accordance with subsection 28.1(1) of the Patent Act, the claim date is the filing date unless there is a compliant request for priority to a previously filed application filed within 12 months and the claimed subject-matter is disclosed in the priority document. Under subsection 28.1(2), where those criteria are satisfied, the claim date is the filing date of the priority document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each claim may have a different claim date in principle. Examiner will verify: (1) whether a compliant request for priority was submitted; (2) the filing date of the priority document to determine timeliness; and (3) the content of the priority document to determine whether the subject-matter of each claim was disclosed in that document. Generalized claims may not benefit from an earlier priority date if the priority document only discloses specific embodiments without support for the broader subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple priority documents — earliest filing date applies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an application claims priority from two or more prior regularly filed applications, subsection 28.4(4) provides that paragraph(s) shall be applied using the earliest filing date of the previously regularly filed applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the earliest possible claim date for subject-matter claimed in the pending application based on content of the earliest corresponding priority document. Examiner must consider content of each priority document to determine which subject-matter benefits from which claim date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority from multiple same-subject-matter prior applications limited by 12-month rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Any application filed more than one year before the filing date of a Canadian application may not form the basis of priority for the Canadian application. Where a first application filed more than 12 months before and a second application with same subject-matter filed within 12 months exist, priority cannot be based on the second application except for subject-matter exclusive to the second application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exception exists under subsection 28.4(5) where the first application was never open to public inspection and will never publish. Examiners are not expected to search for such documents but may encounter them; applicants should ensure appropriate priority basis and provide evidence where relief is claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. continuation and continuation-in-part (CIP) priority rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A United States continuation application has the same specification as an earlier application but contains claims directed to different subject-matter; no new matter is disclosed. A continuation-in-part discloses and claims additional subject-matter over the earlier application. If a Canadian application is filed within one year of a continuation-in-part, that CIP may serve as a priority document for any new matter not disclosed in the original U.S. application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where priority questions arise involving continuations/CIPs, it may be necessary to identify matter derived from the original U.S. application. Because a U.S. CIP does not identify new matter, applicants must submit certified copies of both the original and CIP whenever required. Example provided where priority was denied because original US application's filing date was more than 12 months before Canadian filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace period for applicant-originated disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act provides for a grace period before the filing date during which information that became publicly available due to a disclosure by the applicant, or by a person who obtained knowledge, directly or indirectly, from the applicant, is not considered during the assessment of novelty and inventiveness. The grace period is one year before the filing date (or between claim date and filing date if claim date is earlier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grace period covers oral and written disclosures. In assessing applicability, examiners typically consider shared authorship or same applicant in prior publications and domestic patent documents. Grace period applies when considering anticipation or obviousness, but not when assessing double-patenting. Applicants may provide evidence to support relationship between author of prior disclosure and applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish publication date of prior art reliably
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior disclosure to be considered prior art, the date it became available to the public must generally be known. Where exact date is not known, the disclosure cannot be cited unless a reliable basis exists for concluding it was available before the relevant date (claim date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For publications giving only month/year, cannot presume earlier than last day of month; for year only, cannot presume earlier than December 31. Methods such as third-party internet archiving services may establish earlier actual publication dates. Patent documents usually have known publication dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify content of priority documents (post-Oct 30, 2019)
rubrics_metrics.description: For applications where the request for priority was made on or after October 30, 2019, the content of the priority document can be verified using the copy submitted or made available under subsection 74(1) of the Patent Rules. If examination commences before a copy is submitted, examination should proceed assuming claim date is the filing date until copy is available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should obtain and inspect the submitted priority document to determine whether claimed subject-matter is disclosed. If necessary, request certified copies per Patent Rules where documents are missing or accuracy is in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request translations of foreign-language priority documents only when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: For an examiner to verify content of a priority document filed in a language other than English or French, a translation into English or French may be necessary. Such a request can be made via notice under subsection 76(1) of the Patent Rules. Recognising translation burden, requests should be limited to cases where no viable alternative exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only part of the document is necessary, indicate which part. Examiners should attempt to locate an official-language version or use reliable machine translation (e.g., JPO tool) at early stages. If working from machine translation, state this in the report. Applicants rebutting machine-translation-based arguments may be required to provide an accurate translation. If a submitted translation appears inaccurate, examiner may request translator's statement or new translation under subsection 76(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional consideration for earlier priority requests
rubrics_metrics.description: For requests for priority made before October 30, 2019, the examiner should first attempt to acquire the priority document from a reliable source (e.g., WIPO PATENTSCOPE or International Bureau). Where the priority document is not retrievable or a non-certified copy's accuracy is in doubt, the applicant may be requested under subsection 196(1) of the Patent Rules to provide a certified copy or make it available in a digital library.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow established retrieval steps before requisitioning certified copies; document attempts and deficiencies when requesting applicant assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-patenting doctrine — prohibits multiple patents for same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Double-patenting is the judicially recognised proscription against an applicant being granted more than one patent for a single invention. Jurisprudence recognises two branches: 'same invention' and 'obviousness' double-patenting. Underlying principle: a second patent cannot be justified unless the claims exhibit 'novelty or ingenuity' over the first patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment is a specialised evaluation of anticipation and obviousness where the prior art is an earlier patent by the same applicant; only the claims of the earlier patent are considered. Claims are given purposive construction in light of the specification and common general knowledge on the claim date. Double-patenting applies to the 'same applicant' including legal representatives and applies if the application belonged to the same applicant at any time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlap — identical operating embodiment bars grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlap describes the situation in which an operating embodiment in a claim of an application being examined is identical to an operating embodiment in a claim in an existing patent. The embodiment in the existing patent therefore acts as a bar against the latter; granting that embodiment in two patents would result in double-patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap may involve only a small fraction of claim scope but still creates a defect. Removing the overlap (e.g., deleting duplicated subject-matter) will remove the double-patenting defect. Example: dependent claims that define A+B in both documents can cause overlap unless removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existing patent — issuance bars later non-distinct patents regardless of filing order
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'earlier patent' for double-patenting purposes is a patent that has issued and claims an invention not patentably distinct from that in the application being examined. It is not necessary that the existing patent issued from an application with an earlier filing or claim date than the application being examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office's position: the grant of a further patent defining an invention not patentably distinct from an existing patent is inappropriate regardless of whether the existing patent's rights have expired; issuance can restore rights and thus extend monopoly. Examiner should consider issued patents by same applicant when assessing double-patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-pending applications — notify potential double-patenting but do not delay allowance solely for potential defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two applications belonging to the same applicant define inventions that are not patentably distinct, the examiner will inform the applicant that a potential double-patenting issue exists. This potential defect is not identified in a requisition under section 86 of the Patent Rules, since it is not an actual defect until one of the applications issues to patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application is otherwise in condition for allowance it will not be held back solely because of a potential double-patenting issue. Applicants should exercise care to include all claims to a given invention in a single application. Double-patenting will be identified between an application and an issued patent regardless of whether it was identified while co-pending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division at direction of Office — divisional claims corresponding to examiner-identified groups exempt from double-patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: If an examiner has identified a lack of unity and the applicant files a divisional directed to those identified claims, the claims in the divisional are exempt from examination for double-patenting if they are identical to claims identified by the examiner as lacking unity and differ from those retained in the parent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If divisional claims do not correspond to examiner-identified groupings or are amended to change the claimed invention, they will be examined for double-patenting. Follow procedures in Chapter 21 for unity/division issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selections — three conditions for patentable selection
rubrics_metrics.description: A selection rests on the idea that certain things within a broadly disclosed genus may be different inventions (a species) if based on disclosure of substantial advantages not disclosed by the inventors of the broad invention. The three conditions that must be satisfied for a patentable selection are that: (1) the selection be based on some substantial advantage; (2) the whole of the selection must possess the advantage; and (3) the advantage must be in respect of a quality of a special character peculiar to the whole selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantage must be compared to the overall group and established by sufficient representative testing (not just isolated members). The advantage (or avoidance of a substantial disadvantage) must be properly disclosed; merely stating an embodiment is 'preferred' or has unspecified advantage is insufficient. Selection's utility must be demonstrated or supported by sound prediction; if an operating embodiment within the selection has already been made, the selection is anticipated. Even if not anticipated, selection may be obvious, often assessed by whether the advantage is truly unexpected or under an 'obvious to try' analysis (especially in chemical arts).
